title: Child Prodigies: Better to Burn Out Than Fade Away
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore child prodigies: how they are defined (exceptional mastery by about age ten, usually in one narrow domain), the role of IQ versus working memory, nature and nurture, the "rage to master" concept and Larry Vanderwert's cerebellum theory, studies by Ruthsatz and Urbach on prodigies' working memory and autism traits, famous examples (Mozart's transcription of Allegri's Miserere, John von Neumann, Blaise Pascal, Stevie Wonder, Ramanujan, Venus and Serena Williams, Polgar sisters, Felix and Fanny Mendelssohn), parental roles and pressure cases (Jennifer Capriati, Todd Marinovich, Richard Williams), and the downside of fading after childhood (Bobby Fischer, Elizabeth Benson, Winnifred Sackville Stoner Jr.). The episode closes with a listener mail correction about USAID condom funding.

segments.title: Opening banter and Mozart
segments.summary: Hosts banter about a possible mini episode, then introduce the child prodigies topic and mention the chapter from their book. Chuck introduces Mozart at age fourteen hearing Allegri's Miserere in Vatican City and transcribing it from memory.

segments.title: Defining prodigies versus geniuses
segments.summary: Prodigy is defined as surpassing adult-level mastery by about age ten, usually in one narrow field. Genius is tied to high IQ but does not require achievement. Prodigies were a media sensation in the early twentieth century.

segments.title: Narrow domains and multiple intelligences
segments.summary: Prodigies typically excel in one domain and subsection, and rarely in more than one intelligence type. Chuck connects this to Gardner's multiple intelligences theory from the early 1990s.

segments.title: Nature, nurture, and Ellen Winner
segments.summary: Prodigy development is a mix of nature and nurture. Ellen Winner argues there must be a genetic component and cites a child picking out a tune at age three. Tiger Woods is cited as an example.

segments.title: Prodigy siblings and famous families
segments.summary: Some prodigies have prodigy siblings, such as Maria Mozart, Fanny Mendelssohn, Venus and Serena Williams, and the Polgar sisters. Chuck jokes about a children's book series, and the hosts mention former agent Stephen Barr's children's book.

segments.title: Rage to master
segments.summary: Ellen Winner's term 'rage to master' describes young children who become obsessed with one gift and ignore other activities.

segments.title: Larry Vanderwert's cerebellum theory
segments.summary: Larry Vanderwert links prodigies to connections between the cerebellum and cerebral cortex, describing a feedback loop with reward signals. He argues prodigies depend on culture and suggests they may have first appeared about ten thousand years ago.

segments.title: Working memory and IQ in prodigies
segments.summary: A 2012 study by Ruthsatz and Urbach of eight prodigies found all were in the 99th percentile for working memory, while IQs were not extreme. Working memory is explained as useful for chess, math, and music.

segments.title: Working memory examples and 2014 study
segments.summary: John von Neumann reciting phone book pages is cited as an example of working memory. Josh describes Kevin Pollak mouthing comedy records as a child. A 2014 study of eighteen prodigies in math, music, and art found different patterns of working memory and visual-spatial skills.

segments.title: Autism connection and savants
segments.summary: Prodigies in the 2012 study had more autistic relatives and high attention to detail scores but not elevated scores elsewhere. Chuck notes that people with severe autism or other differences are classed as savants rather than prodigies.

segments.title: Parents and resources
segments.summary: Parents play a major role through resources, expert teachers, and timing. Josh mentions Wolfgang Van Halen as a prodigy with a built-in teacher. Chuck notes Picasso's father was an art instructor.

segments.title: Prodigies without resources
segments.summary: Blaise Pascal reinvented geometry after his father hid math books, and later developed probability theory. Stevie Wonder and Srinivasa Ramanujan are cited as prodigies who overcame poverty and taught themselves.

segments.title: Pushy parents and burnout
segments.summary: Todd Marinovich and Jennifer Capriati were pushed by overbearing parents and burned out. Richard Williams turned Venus pro at fourteen before a proposed USTA rule, and she debuted against a top player.

segments.title: Fading after childhood
segments.summary: Prodigies may face a fall once they are no longer special. Bobby Fischer is the cautionary example, with a collapse after becoming a grandmaster at fifteen. Elizabeth Benson, who went to college at twelve, later lived a normal life, and Winnifred Sackville Stoner Jr. was pushed by her mother. The hosts give advice to parents.

segments.title: Closing banter on parenting and Christmas letters
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the difficulty for parents and joke about Christmas letters bragging about children. Chuck mentions a band named Rage to Master.

segments.title: Listener mail: USAID condom correction
segments.summary: Listener Bernie F. Chavis corrects an earlier episode: the fifty million dollars in condoms was for Gaza Province in Mozambique, not the Gaza Strip. The hosts thank him.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard closing credits and listener mail address.
